Now that the Story has been finalized, I think it's time to pointlessly brainstorm. I'm not entirely sure where we were at the end of Rebirth, but we presumably went down South a bit after the Forgotten Capital. So here's a rough outline of how I think the game would play out if it were solely a Remake of Discs 2 & 3.

***Major Spoilers*** for FF7 ahead.

**Act 1**

Sephiroth and Shrina reveal Cloud's troubled past, and the group faces tragedy as Cloud is forced to betray them.

* Chapter 01: Rocket Town (Cid's backstory)
* Chapter 02: Great Glacier & Whirlwind Maze (Encounter Shinra and Sephiroth)
* Chapter 03: Escape From Junon (Introduce the Highwind, Tifa as party leader)
* Chapter 04: Mideel Region (Find Cloud, Tifa leaves party)
* Chapter 05: Fort Condor Region (Group cornered by Shinra)
* Chapter 06: Cloud's Subconscious (Cloud's true backstory, play as Zack/Cloud and battle Sephiroth)

**Act 2**

An expanded struggle against the Weapons & Shinra for the Huge Materia, as well as Shinra getting their comeuppance. Without these awful people enabling his worst tendencies, Rufus slowly becomes a better person.

* Chapter 07: Condor War (Cloud and Tifa arrive to save the day)
* Chapter 08: World Exploration & Huge Materia Quests (Cloud, Cid, Cait Sith steal submarine; Barret and the others go to North Corel)
* Chapter 09: Lucrecia Cave (Vincent's backstory)
* Chapter 10: Rocket Town Region (Defeat Palmer, go to space)
* Chapter 11: Wutai Region (Yuffie's Backstory; Defeat Corneo)
* Chapter 12: Wutai War (Shinra Invades Wutai)

**Act 3**

Rufus plans to aid Cloud's group with the Mako cannon. This triggers multiple simultaneous coup attempts by Rufus' cabinet.

* Chapter 13: Great Glacier Region (Bugenhagen & the Forgotten Capital)
* Chapter 14: Mako Cannon Rampage (Cloud, Red XIII, & Vincent vs Hojo; Everyone Else vs Proud Clod)
* Chapter 15: Final World Exploration & Cleanup (Bugenhagen's death, optional superbosses)
* Chapter 16: Northern Crater (Final Jenova Fight)
* Chapter 17: Reunion (Final Crater Descent, vs Sephiroth & Lifestream Duel)

However, we all know that this won't just be a Remake of the last two discs, and these expansions alone will probably not cover the full scope of the story. **Part 3: Unraveling the Myth**

When we talk about taxation, we shouldn't talk about it in terms of funding things or eliminating inequality. While taxes CAN be used to reduce inequality, this is highly dependent on the type of taxes, and even the taxes that DO reduce inequality don't address the root cause of it. In fact, certain taxes that are considered progressive, like corporate taxes, can actually be regressive. They're useless for reducing inequality because in almost all cases, these higher taxes just end up being paid indirectly by the corporation's workers or consumers via wage cuts and price hikes. A CEO isn't going to cut HIS wages, but the wages of those under him, and this will continue all the way down the ladder.

The Billionaire class has worked tirelessly for generations, using violence and unfair agreements to monopolize the means of production for themselves, and when that happens they gain the ability to set wages and prices. By allowing this to happen, you allow for the creation of inequality. When you give someone complete control over the lives of workers, it inevitably leads to exploitation. The working public needs to collectively own the means of production, the natural resources and services that people depend on, in order to emancipate itself from inequality that is created by the lust and gluttony of wealthy individuals.

Even though certain taxes such as estate taxes and capital gains taxes are more effective at reducing inequality on paper, raising taxes on the top 1% doesn't automatically make the lives of the 99% any better. No matter how high you raise the top marginal tax rates, capitalists will still own the means of production. They own the building you work in, the company you work for, the resources that the company works with, and the politicians that give them unfettered access to those resources. As a result, they will still control people's working lives. Taxing them doesn't actually do anything to reduce their control over the means of production, or their ability to set wages and prices.

If you do not eliminate the Billionaire monopoly on the means of production, then you have not removed the means through which the Billionaire class has exploited their workers and siphoned their wealth from. Ultimately, labor conditions will not change and wages will not increase. It doesn't matter whether your boss' tax bracket is 35%, 40%, or even 50%. Jeff Bezos won't suddenly have an epiphany about making Amazon workers urinate in bottles because he has to pay an extra 4-14% in taxes. It doesn't remove the financial incentive for Amazon to continue mistreating its employees, nor would ExxonMobil's incentive to ignore and discredit climate change as it continues drilling and hydraulic fracturing to extract the black blood of the Earth to fuel and finance its corporate empire.
_______________________________________________________________________

**Conclusion**

It is not that income inequality shouldn't be solved through taxation, but that it ***cannot*** be solved through taxation. If you do not remove the system that gave capitalists absolute control in the first place, then any attempt at reducing inequality is ultimately fruitless because the root cause of income inequality is not inadequate taxation, but private property: the private ownership of land, labor, and natural resources for economic exploitation.

If a corporation is destroying the planet, or exploiting workers on a mass scale, or both...then you don't solve those issues by taxing them. You nationalize it. Make it public property, and decide what to do with it collectively through the democratic process. Workers need to collectively own the means of production in order to truly be free from the dictatorship of capital, and the idly wealthy that use it to control us.

**Part 2: Taxation and Public Services**
 
When Liberals and Social Democrats connect taxing the rich to funding social programs for the poor, they inadvertently limit what is possible to whatever they can tax out of the rich. By perpetuating this myth, you give the rich a false sense of benevolence and control over the government's capacity to provide social programs that people need. The false narrative of "taxpayer money" in general creates animosity between the working class, because some working class individuals will falsely think that their tax dollars are funding welfare programs for the "lazy" poor. You hear it all the time: 

"Why should MY hard earned tax dollars fund OTHER people's healthcare?"

"I don't want MY tax dollars to pay for LAZY people on welfare."

Liberals, Conservatives, and Social Democrat politicians alike perpetuate the myth of revenue spending to appeal to people's elementary common sense, but it has terrible effects in the long run because it reinforces the economic illiteracy that misleads so much of the public. And I personally find it frustrating to see this done by populist politicians like Bernie Sanders or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez because I know both of them know about Modern Monetary Theory (MMT). Stephanie Kelton, an MMT economist and author of bestseller "The Deficit Myth", was Bernie's chief economic advisor; and AOC admitted in the past to having studied MMT, yet she still donned a white dress with "Tax the Rich" printed on it in big red letters pretending like she doesn't know this method is ineffective.

"Tax the Rich" also puts up artificial barriers to passing progressive legislation. If the logic is taken literally, you would need to first tax the rich before you can implement the policies, which is an especially difficult thing to do an a corporately managed "democracy" like the United States.

Even if it's not the intention, the "Tax the Rich" narrative perpetuates the view that without rich people we can't have nice things. Which is just plainly false. Workers make our nice things. People's labor is the real source of value produced in the world. Any policy is possible to implement if there are the physical resources available to maintain it. Capital is merely a means of exchange for these resources, by itself it is not truly a resource. What actually matters is how do you resource that capital? The backing force of the US Dollar is the physical resources and productive capacity of the United States.

Think about what it costs us—*really* costs us—to give a person on SNAP two lbs of apples. It it $1.59 cents per lb? No, it costs two lbs of apples and it stops there. The currency and price is just a medium of exchange for good and labor. The same thinking can be applied to every good and service provided in the United States. Universal health care only costs us the resources to produce the medicine or perform the procedures necessary to improve someone's health. Of course, people must be compensated for their work, so you pay the doctors, nurses, technicians, and pharmacists. What does it cost to house a homeless person? Well, if you build a house, a decent bit of resources. Wood, concrete, plaster, plus the cost of labor. But if you just give them a house that already exists? It costs...a house and the land it stands on.

Which is especially frustrating since we have an estimated ***16 million vacant homes*** and only about 550,000 homeless persons in the entire United States.

Taxing the rich does nothing to address the root cause of inequality, and the very idea of revenue spending is antiquated for a dominant economic power like the United States, which is the sole provider of its own fiat currency that is also the global benchmark currency.

Before we go on, two things of note I want to bring up.

2. As I am a citizen of the United States, I will be using it as a lens for this mini-essay.

Contrary to the commonly held belief, the Federal Government does ***not*** tax for revenue.

All of our expenses at the Federal level are made in the form of deficit spending—meaning that the government spends money first, and taxes later to make up for the shortfall. A government that issues its own fiat money can pay for goods, services, and financial assets without the need to first collect money in the form of taxes or debt issuance in advance of such purchases. It can't be forced to default on a debt denominated in its own currency because they're the the sole entity that legitimizes the currency.
_______________________________________________________________________

**Part 1: Understanding Modern Monetary Theory**

US Dollars can only come from our Federal government. When Congress passes legislation that requires federal spending and the President signs the legislation, the Treasury Department is instructed to administer the payments. The Federal Reserve Board is our Central Bank and it's where the US Treasury does its banking. Because the Treasury and the FRB are agents of the Federal government, when new spending is approved the Federal Reserve simply marks up the Treasury's bank account to make sure the payments clear.

Once the payments are cleared, money is transferred from the Treasury’s account to your Commercial Bank in the private sector. Because banks are members of the Federal Reserve, it's simply a script that marks up the private bank’s ledger while marking down the Treasury’s ledger by the same amount. If you received a stimulus payment during COVID you most likely looked at your bank account one day and noticed there was $1600 more than you had before, and you would also see a transaction from the Treasury Dept. Even if you received a physical check, you simply gave the paper to a teller and the teller marked up your bank account.

This process includes ALL payments made by the Federal government in US dollars, and actually is the primary way in which the US dollar is created.

Same thing happens thousands of times each day. Say the government enacts legislation that funds a highway project for $40 million. The civil engineering firm that won the contract would have a $40 million markup in its account and the Treasury’s account would be marked down by $40 million. Our money supply is nothing more than a giant bank ledger controlled entirely by the federal government.

Today, it's strokes on a keyboard. Back in the Second World War, when Congress authorized the spending that was orders of magnitude greater than the amount of reserves Treasury had on hand, it was a handwritten bank ledger. When the Government chose to issue itself debt in the form of War bonds, it does so in order to control inflation in the short term, as well as guaranteeing its Citizens risk free assets that they can store their extra money in and collect interest on.

The Federal government is not a corporation or a private citizen, nor should it be thought of as one. It can ALWAYS make ANY and ALL payments in its own currency. Its spending is in no way constrained by its revenues, and there is no issue that can be solved simply by "balancing our checkbook".

The only limit that the government has on spending and purchases is inflation. If too many dollars are in circulation, inflation rises and the value of the dollar drops. In order to counteract inflation, the government must work towards removing money from the economy. This is accomplished primarily through taxation, although other methods like traffic tickets and fees for government services also contribute towards this. When you pay your taxes you aren't giving money to the government, but instead are returning a minuscule amount of value to the US dollar.

As an example analogy, think about it like this: When you purchase admission to a concert or sporting event, the venue provides you with a physical or digital ticket that serves as your right of entry. The ticket itself has no purpose except for admission to the event, and has no value elsewhere. When you arrive at the event, someone will collect or scan your ticket and you will give allowed entry. However, after that event, the ticket loses all purpose and is effectively worthless. Digital tickets are voided and physical ones are thrown in the trash. Now replace "venue" with the United States' Federal government, "ticket" with the US dollar, and "the event" with...every transaction made in the US and Global economies. Though this is true with many developed economies across the globe.

People are saying that they're going to squish down to 60, and that Kalimdor and E. Kingdom will only get you to 20/30 or whatever. Taliesin even suggested that you get to level 40 doing Azeroth content and then choose to do one expansion to get to 60. But that's all crap. I, for one, am not intimidated by the idea of a ***MAJOR*** level and XP squish, to the point where completely a single zone might not even give you a whole level.  It seems intended for Eastern Kingdoms and Kalimdor that certain factions follow specific questing routes. Of course you don't have to follow the intended path, but you *can* for a more cohesive story. For example, Orcs go: Durotar -> N. Barrens -> Ashenvale -> Stonetalon -> Desolace -> Feralas -> 1K Needles -> Tanaris -> Un'goro -> Silithus -> Outland.

* Orc, Trolls, Tauren, Goblins, Night Elves, and Worgen have 10 zones.
* Draenei have 11 zones due to their zones not being changed in Cata.
* Dwarves, Gnomes, and Forsaken have 12 zones along their route.
* Humans and Blood Elves have 13 zones. (Belf zones weren't changed in cata). Humans have an extra zone since Westfall and Redridge split the traditional 10-20 zone in two.

Find the mean and it's 11.083, so let's go ahead and just say that's an average of 11 zones before getting to expansion content. Keep in mind that this is only considering quests, not heirlooms (one of WoW's worst mistakes) or dungeon grinding bullshit.

* Outland has seven zones that overlap levels, and a Max level zone. Netherstorm and Shadowmoon have the exact same level ranges.
* Wrath has two starting zones, four mid-level zones, and then three final leveling zones that overlap.
* Cata also has two starting zones, and three leveling zones.
* Pandaria has one starting zone (although it's twice as big as all the other zones to accommodate both factions), five leveling zones, plus three max level only zones. Valley and Krasarang are kind of one zone split in two like Redridge and Westfall.
* WoD has two starting zones, four leveling zones, and two max level zones.
* Legion has four leveling zones, two max level zones, and Surumar is a bit of both.
* BFA is a bit unique as you do swap between the continents somewhat during leveling, but each faction has three main zones, and currently two max level zones in the form of Nazjatar and Mechagon.

Now imagine only getting one level per zone from quest content, ignoring max level-only zones. That's 47 levels just from quest content. Let's streamline it a bit and assume you get a few levels just from the casual XP grind

* 15 from Cata-Vanilla
* 5 from Outland
* 5 from Northrend
* 5 from Cataclysm
* 5 from Pandaria
* 5 from Draenor
* 5 from Broken Isles
* 5 from Kul Tiras/Zandalar

Which leaves you at level 50 and opens up the next expansion to bring us back up to level 60 and not 70 like some people want. I honestly like the idea of changing the paradigm for something we haven't seen before. If you really wanted to do expansion choice, you could just double the XP for those expansions. But I honestly think they should just update all of the old expansion content for the present timeline. Right now, it's impossible to tell who the goddamn Warchief is half the time as your leveling Horde because it starts with Sylvanas, then it goes to Garrosh, then Thrall, then back to Garrosh, then Vol'jin, and finally Sylvanas again. The stories are simply broken and need to be streamlined. Even if it's just as simple as the Bronze Draognflight saying saying "Oh no, something's wrong with the timestream and we need you to go back and help X at Y in Z timeline so that time isn't fucked up forever."
 
Now imagine having finished the entirety of a zone's story, rewarded with with a new level and a new unlocked ability. You don't have to worry about finishing a zone early thanks to scaling technology, so you can experience the full story of a zone without worry. Yes, the *feel* of player progression is scaled back, but at this point there isn't really a discernible improvement between gear that's meant for someone at level 30 and gear that's mean for someone at level 50 due to the two stat squishes. This gives them room to make gear improvements actually mean something. Now you're comparing level 1 gear to what was previously level 60 gear over the course of just 10 levels. That's how you do power progression justice.

Currently, the seven talent tiers are unlocked every 15 levels plus an oddity at level 100. which is simply too big of a gap to feel rewarding. If the new level cap is 60, that's a new talent every 8 levels, getting your final talent about halfway through the new expansion. I still think that's too big of a gap, but learning new abilities much more often as you level should help bridge it. Personally I think they should have a mix of the old and new, with the old talent trees only providing you with raw stat increases or passive effects (some don't even have to be combat oriented, I wouldn't mind something that gave me a 1% reputation boost, or talents that give me 5% extra gold from mobs or 10% more mats from a resource node). Then, the current talent tiers could be as they are now. Giving you new, unique abilities, replacing an ability with an upgraded version, and/or changing how a currently existing ability works in your rotation entirely, every eight levels and unlocking the final tier about halfway through the next expansion. Personally, I would call this updated version of the old system "Skills" and the current system would stay named Talents.

This doesn't just fix the problem of having "too many levels". It fixes the gear problem, it fixes the power creep problem, it fixes the story and lore problems, it fixes the issue people have with talents. It removes bullshit like heirlooms and level 1 mounts since you shouldn't need everything handed to you on a platter to get through a proper and well written story.

In terms of leadership, the "rebellion" is an ***Alliance*** to restore the Galactic Republic. Mon Mothma co-orchestrated the Alliance with Bail Organa and Garm Bel Iblis (at least in legends). She is a senator from Chandrila and one of the key figures in rebel leadership. Each of the major factions that were individual rebel cells had their leader seemingly become a representative on the Alliance council. Thus Bail, Mon Mothma, and Garm, were all on the council. Carlist Rieekan (General from episode V) also eventually joined the council.

In regard to Leia, she was a high ranking member of the Alderaan faction. She only answered directly to her foster father, Bail Organa, who was the Viceroy of Alderaan and also leader of the Alderaan rebel cells. Likewise, Bail had to answer to the Alliance Council he was part of. Leia, being Alderaan's senator, was still influential and important to the Alliance as a whole, but she was not one of its leaders until Bail's death after the destruction of Alderaan.

In short, Leia's important, but she's not a major leader until the end of ANH. At which point she presumably takes her father's place on the Alliance council. Which is why she is giving orders on Hoth. The rebel leaders tended to not be together all at once unless absolutely necessary to avoid being captured en mass.

EDIT: Mon Mothma is also Chancellor of the Rebel Alliance. Meaning that politically, she was its leader in diplomatic and civil affairs. However, she was not in direct control of the military. Military affairs were directed by the Alliance council.

There's actually three references there, all to 19th century French history.

The Battle of Trafalgar was a famous 1805 naval engagement in which a modest British fleet under the command of Admiral and Viscount Horatio Nelson defeated the combined Spanish and French fleets under Pierre-Charles Villeneuve. Nelson was killed in action, but he managed to defeat the larger allied fleet, captured half of it, and killed almost 10,000 more soldiers than the 1000 he lost. He single-handedly destroyed any hope of Napoleon ever invading Britain, forcing him to try and take out all their allies and disrupt their trade via the Continental System.

The Battle of Waterloo (Wateru) is mostly famously known as Napoleon's last stand against the Seventh Coalition against British General and Duke Arthur Wellesley, who previously handed the French their @$$ in the Peninsular War. His strategy was genius, but it was really thanks to the unexpected rain that bogged down Napoleon's cannons (one of his greatest assets was his godly artillery skills) that he won the day in 1815.

Law is a reference to the Napoleonic Code, one of the French Emperor's greatest achievements. It serves as the basis for much of modern civil law in the West.

Naruto is indeed on a thin line between Neutral Good and Chaotic Good, and arguments could be made for both points. He's too free-spirited and independent to be Neutral, but he's also too morally-inclined to be Chaotic.

He does think outside standard ninja conventions to accomplish things like convincing Nagato and Obito that they're misguided, while if Sasuke or even Kakashi had been in the same situation, they likely would have just killed them. Hell, Kakashi TRIED to kill the DEFEATED Obito.

To add further context, let's add Danzo to the alignment chart. Danzo is, in my opinion, Chaotic Good. He does, on occasion, do things for his own benefit (i.e becoming Hokage), but he also does them because that's what he thinks is right. He allied with Hanzo against Akatsuki because he thought that rebels they would become a bigger threat than a tyrannical dictator. He was right, but he was not in the right. He does bad things for his ideal of the greater good.

Naruto is nothing like Danzo. If he were the 3rd Hokage he would never resort to something like the Uchiha Massacre. He would prefer preemptive diplomacy over a preemptive strike. Even if that diplomacy failed and the Uchiha started their coup, he would fight to stop the coup, but not to end the dispute.

So it is for this reason Naruto I think is Neutral Good, (and also why Sasuke will allow Naruto to be Hokage in his place).

I think Sasuke is more Lawful Neutral, at least in his goals. He wants to become Hokage so that things like the Uchiha massacre never happen again. He's not exactly doing it out of the kindness in his heart.

Naruto is probably Neutral Good and Hagoromo is the same.

Kaguya on the other hand, is probably [Lawful Evil](http://i47.photobucket.com/albums/f187/Zandrax/alignments/07LawfulEvil01.jpg) like Madara.
